prompt: Explain the federal budget using only football metaphors. Do not stop when they stop working.
response:
The federal budget is a never-ending football game where the scoreboard is dollars, the clock is politics, and everyone insists they’re “just trying to win,” even while arguing about what sport this is.

## The field and the teams
Congress is the home team offense and also the home team defense, because it writes the plays and then tries to stop the consequences of its own play-calling. The President is the head coach with a challenge flag (veto) and a headset full of advisors. Federal agencies are the position groups: linemen at Treasury, receivers at Health and Human Services, special teams at FEMA, and a defensive backfield at the FBI trying to prevent long bombs of chaos.

Voters are the owners, except the owners meet once every two years, yell about clock management, and then replace the kicker.

## The playbook (the budget)
The budget is the playbook everyone waves around in the pregame show. It’s full of bold arrows and confident commentary, but it’s not the final call on the field. It’s the “game plan” that says, “We’re going to establish the run,” while everyone knows the first snap will be a screen pass to reality.

## Revenue is offense: taxes are yardage
Taxes are the offense moving the chains. Income tax is the steady run game: not flashy, but it keeps the drive alive. Payroll taxes are the fullback dive: repetitive, bruising, and somehow always on 3rd-and-short. Corporate taxes are the deep shot: fans remember the highlights, but it’s inconsistent and the wind matters. Tariffs are a trick play that also clotheslines your own receiver.

Economic growth is yards after catch: when it happens, everyone claims they drew it up.

## Spending is the drives: programs are formations
Spending is how the team advances downfield toward “public goals,” which are end zones that keep getting moved because someone put them on wheels.

- Social Security is the veteran running back: still productive, huge fanbase, expensive contract, and everyone promises they’ll “build around him.”
- Medicare and Medicaid are the hurry-up offense: fast, necessary, and draining the defense’s lungs.
- Defense spending is the pass rush: costly, relentless, and always justified by the other team’s offense, whether or not you can see them on the sideline.
